Question: For each positive integer \(n,\) let \(S(n)\) be the number of sequences of length \(n\) consisting solely of the letters \(A\) and \(B,\) with no more than three \(A\)s in a row and no more than three \(B\)s in a row. What is the remainder when \(S(2015)\) is divided by \(12?\)
Solution:
The useful feature to track is the last uninterrupted run of equal letters. For \(n\ge4\), this run has length \(j=1,2,\) or \(3\). Deleting the whole last run leaves a nonempty valid sequence of length \(n-j\). Conversely, any valid sequence of length \(n-j\) has exactly one extension whose final run has length \(j\): append \(j\) copies of the letter opposite to its last letter. These three cases are disjoint and include every valid sequence. Therefore
\[
S(n)=S(n-1)+S(n-2)+S(n-3)\qquad(n\ge4).
\]
Every sequence of length at most three is allowed, so
\[
S(1)=2,\qquad S(2)=4,\qquad S(3)=8.
\]

To find a remainder modulo \(12\), we can first find the remainders modulo \(4\) and modulo \(3\). Reducing each recurrence calculation modulo \(4\) gives
\[
(S(1),\ldots,S(7))
\equiv(2,0,0,2,2,0,0)\pmod4.
\]
The triple at positions \(5,6,7\) equals the triple at positions \(1,2,3\). Since three consecutive terms determine every following term, this proves that the residues repeat with period \(4\). As \(2015=4\cdot503+3\),
\[
S(2015)\equiv S(3)\equiv0\pmod4.
\]

The corresponding calculations modulo \(3\) give
\[
(S(1),\ldots,S(8))
\equiv(2,1,2,2,2,0,1,0)\pmod3,
\]
\[
(S(9),\ldots,S(16))
\equiv(1,2,0,0,2,2,1,2)\pmod3.
\]
Now the triple at positions \(14,15,16\) equals the initial triple. The same recurrence argument proves period \(13\). Since \(2015=13\cdot154+13\),
\[
S(2015)\equiv S(13)\equiv2\pmod3.
\]
The remainders between \(0\) and \(11\) divisible by \(4\) are \(0,4,8\). Only \(8\) has remainder \(2\) upon division by \(3\). Thus the requested remainder is \(\boxed{8}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
